recipe: Always access Embind-exposed objects through the Module object rather than the global namespace, since the closure compiler or wrapping may hide them from the global scope.
trigger_condition: You are calling Embind-exposed functions or classes from JavaScript code.
evidence: Always access objects through the :ref:`module` object, as shown above.

recipe: Bind only the C++ members that JavaScript actually needs, since each binding increases the compiled code size.
trigger_condition: You are writing an EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS block for a class with many methods or properties.
evidence: As a rule you should bind only those items that are actually needed, as each binding increases the code size.

recipe: When your JavaScript is processed by the closure compiler (e.g. via --pre-js, --post-js, EM_ASM, EM_JS, or --closure 1), use bracket notation like Module["MyClass"] instead of dot notation to prevent symbol renaming from breaking Embind bindings.

recipe: Explicitly call delete() on every C++ object handle you receive from JavaScript, whether constructed directly or returned from a C++ method, unless a reference return value policy is in use.
trigger_condition: Your JavaScript code creates or receives C++ object handles from Embind bindings.
evidence: It is strongly recommended that JavaScript code explicitly deletes any C++ object handles it has received.

recipe: Wrap C++ object handle usage in a try/finally block so that delete() is called on every code path, including early returns and thrown exceptions.
trigger_condition: A C++ object handle is used across multiple code paths that may return early or throw.
evidence: The ``try`` … ``finally`` JavaScript construct can be used to guarantee C++ object handles are deleted for all code paths, regardless of early returns or errors thrown.

recipe: Declare short-lived Embind C++ handles with `using obj = new Module.MyClass()` so they are deleted automatically at end of scope; this needs a JS engine or transpiler that supports explicit resource management (`using`/Symbol.dispose). Otherwise use try/finally with delete().
trigger_condition: A C++ object is only needed within a single scope and you want automatic cleanup without manual delete().
evidence: It allows to automatically delete short-lived C++ objects at the end of the scope when they're declared with a `using` keyword
_original_recipe: Declare short-lived C++ object handles with the using keyword to let Embind automatically delete them at the end of scope.
_review_reason: using-declaration needs a JS runtime/toolchain with explicit resource management; say so

recipe: Use value_array and value_object bindings for basic types so that JavaScript Arrays and Objects are converted automatically, eliminating the need for manual lifetime management of primitive data.
trigger_condition: You need to pass or return simple data structures (e.g. structs with primitive fields) between C++ and JavaScript.
evidence: Manual memory management for basic types is onerous, so *embind* provides support for value types.

recipe: When generating Embind bindings from a static library (.a), force the linker to keep the object so the EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS static constructors run: `emcc -lembind -o lib.js -Wl,--whole-archive libfoo.a -Wl,--no-whole-archive`.
trigger_condition: You are building bindings for a .a library file rather than a single source file.
evidence: when generating bindings for library files the compiler must be explicitly instructed to include the object file.
_original_recipe: When generating bindings for a pre-compiled library archive, pass --whole-archive to emcc so the linker includes the object file and the static constructors in the EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS block actually run.
_review_reason: the flag is a linker flag passed via -Wl and must bracket the archive

recipe: Run any JavaScript that depends on Embind-exposed symbols inside the onRuntimeInitialized callback, since the runtime (and thus the bindings) is not ready until WebAssembly compilation finishes.
trigger_condition: Your JavaScript code calls Embind-exposed functions or classes at load time.
evidence: We use the ``onRuntimeInitialized`` callback to run code when the runtime is ready, which is an asynchronous operation (in order to compile WebAssembly).

recipe: Use return_value_policy instead of allow_raw_pointers when binding a function that returns a raw pointer.
trigger_condition: When binding a C++ function whose return type is a raw pointer.
evidence: If the function returns a pointer it is recommended to use a :cpp:type:`return_value_policy` instead of the general :cpp:type:`allow_raw_pointers`.

recipe: Embind requires raw pointers in bound signatures to be marked with allow_raw_pointers() or a return_value_policy; for functions that RETURN a pointer, prefer a return_value_policy (take_ownership or reference) over allow_raw_pointers().
trigger_condition: When a bound function accepts or returns raw pointers.
evidence: Because raw pointers have unclear lifetime semantics, *embind* requires their use to be marked with either :cpp:type:`allow_raw_pointers` or with a :cpp:type:`return_value_policy`.
_original_recipe: Mark raw pointer usage with either allow_raw_pointers or a return_value_policy in your bindings.
_review_reason: merged with :9 so the rule and the preferred choice are in one hint

recipe: Specialize the smart_ptr_trait template to teach embind about custom smart pointer templates.
trigger_condition: When using a custom smart pointer template that embind does not natively recognize.
evidence: To teach *embind* about custom smart pointer templates, you must specialize the :cpp:type:`smart_ptr_trait` template.

recipe: Annotate pure virtual function bindings with pure_virtual so JavaScript subclasses get a helpful error if they forget to override the method.
trigger_condition: When binding pure virtual C++ functions that JavaScript classes are expected to override.
evidence: The :cpp:type:`pure_virtual` annotation on the function binding allows JavaScript to throw a helpful error if the JavaScript class does not override ``invoke()``. Otherwise, you may run into confusing errors.

recipe: Avoid defining class fields that correspond to regular C++ bindings (such as class_<T>) because they follow C++ lifetime rules and may require explicit cleanup in JavaScript.
trigger_condition: When defining class fields in embind bindings for a C++ class.
evidence: It is not recommended to use fields that correspond to regular C++ binding (such as ``class_<T>``) since those properties will obey the normal lifetime rules of their bound type and may require explicit cleanup in JavaScript.

recipe: Control ownership of a C++ object returned to JS by passing a policy to function/method/property bindings: return_value_policy::take_ownership() (JS owns it and must delete()) or return_value_policy::reference() (C++ keeps ownership; do not delete from JS).
trigger_condition: When you need to control what happens to a C++ object returned to JavaScript.
evidence: To use a return value policy, pass the desired policy into function, method, or property bindings.
_original_recipe: Pass the desired return value policy directly into function, method, or property bindings to control C++ object lifetime when returning to JavaScript.

recipe: When a C++ class has a non-pure virtual function that can be overridden but doesn't have to, use a wrapper class with `allow_subclass` and bind the virtual function with `optional_override` to avoid infinite mutual recursion between the wrapper and JavaScript.
trigger_condition: A C++ class has a non-pure virtual function with a default implementation that JavaScript subclasses may or may not override.
evidence: The special lambda binding for invoke is necessary to avoid infinite mutual recursion between the wrapper and JavaScript.

recipe: To establish inheritance relationships in embind, use the `base<BaseClass>` template parameter when binding a derived class, which makes base class member functions accessible and allows derived instances to be passed where base instances are expected.
trigger_condition: You need to expose a C++ class hierarchy with inheritance to JavaScript.
evidence: Any member functions defined on ``BaseClass`` are then accessible to instances of ``DerivedClass``. In addition, any function that accepts an instance of ``BaseClass`` can be given an instance of ``DerivedClass``.

recipe: When exposing raw binary data to JavaScript via typed arrays, treat the memory view like a raw pointer: the runtime does not manage its lifetime or validity, so ensure the underlying buffer outlives the view to avoid data corruption.
trigger_condition: You are using `typed_memory_view` to expose a C++ buffer as a JavaScript typed array.
evidence: Memory views should be treated like raw pointers; lifetime and validity are not managed by the runtime and it's easy to corrupt data if the underlying object is modified or deallocated.

recipe: Use emscripten::val::global to obtain the symbol for a JavaScript global object, emscripten::val::new_ to instantiate it, and emscripten::val::set to configure its properties before use.
trigger_condition: When you need to interact with a JavaScript global object (e.g., AudioContext) from C++ via embind.
evidence: First we use :cpp:func:`~emscripten::val::global` to get the symbol for the global ``AudioContext`` object.  We then use :cpp:func:`~emscripten::val::new_` to create the context

recipe: Link Embind with `-lembind` (older Emscripten used `--bind`), e.g. `emcc -O2 -lembind -o out.js src.cpp`; without it the EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS symbols are unresolved.
trigger_condition: When building a C++ project that uses embind bindings for JavaScript interop.
evidence: emcc -O2 -Wall -Werror -lembind -o oscillator.html oscillator.cpp
_original_recipe: Compile your embind C++ project with emcc using the -lembind flag to produce a working HTML output file.
_review_reason: overstated: -lembind is needed for any Embind build, not just HTML output; note older --bind

recipe: Call register_vector, register_map, or register_optional inside your EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS block to enable automatic conversion between C++ STL containers and JavaScript.
trigger_condition: When your C++ code uses std::vector, std::map, or std::optional and you need them accessible from JavaScript.
evidence: For convenience, *embind* provides factory functions to register ``std::vector<T, class Allocator=std::allocator<T>>`` (:cpp:func:`register_vector`)

recipe: Generate TypeScript definition files by invoking emcc with the --emit-tsd option to produce .d.ts files from your EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS blocks.
trigger_condition: When you want type-safe TypeScript interfaces for your embind C++ bindings.
evidence: Embind supports generating TypeScript definition files from :cpp:func:`EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS` blocks. To generate **.d.ts** files invoke *emcc* with the :ref:`embind-emit-tsd <emcc-emit-tsd>` option

recipe: Use EMSCRIPTEN_DECLARE_VAL_TYPE combined with register_type to provide custom TypeScript type information for emscripten::val parameters, which default to any.
trigger_condition: When your API uses emscripten::val types and you want better TypeScript type safety than the default any.
evidence: To give better type information, custom `val` types can be registered using :cpp:func:`EMSCRIPTEN_DECLARE_VAL_TYPE` in combination with :cpp:class:`emscripten::register_type`

recipe: Add the nonnull<ret_val>() policy parameter to a function binding when the C++ function is guaranteed to return a valid object, to omit | null from generated TypeScript definitions.
trigger_condition: When a C++ function is guaranteed to return a non-null pointer and you want cleaner TypeScript types without null checks.
evidence: If the C++ function is guaranteed to return a valid object, then a policy parameter of ``nonnull<ret_val>()`` can be added to the function binding to omit ``| null`` from TS.
